blocks.text: There's a moment most D2C founders eventually have. You open Meta Ads Manager and it tells you that you did 4.2x ROAS last month. You feel good. Then you open your bank account, look at what actually landed, subtract ad spend, and the math doesn't come close to agreeing.
The dashboard and the bank account are telling two different stories. The bank account is the one that pays your salary.
This post explains exactly why that gap exists, why it's structural rather than a bug, and how to get to a number you can actually trust.
The dashboard-vs-bank-account gap is not a glitch

It helps to understand what a platform like Meta is actually measuring. When someone buys from you, Meta asks a simple question: did this person see or click one of our ads within the attribution window? If yes, Meta books the sale as a Meta conversion.

The problem is that Google asks the exact same question about the same buyer. So does TikTok. So does your email platform. A customer who saw a Meta ad on Monday, clicked a Google search ad on Wednesday, and finally bought after an email on Friday gets counted once in each of those four dashboards. That's one sale reported four times.

Nobody is lying on purpose. Each platform is honestly reporting touches within its own window. But none of them can see the others, so they all take full credit. Stack the dashboards and you've manufactured revenue that doesn't exist.
How big is the overlap?

Across the brands HypeOn has reconciled, roughly 31% of conversions are claimed by two or more channels simultaneously. Put differently: about a third of the "wins" in your individual platform reports are being counted more than once somewhere in your stack.

blocks.text: That single fact reframes every performance conversation you've ever had. The 4.2x ROAS isn't a target you hit — it's a number inflated by an accounting overlap you never agreed to.
The three forces inflating your reported ROAS
Double-counting is the biggest culprit, but it works alongside two others.

items: **Generous attribution windows.** Meta's default click-and-view windows are wide enough that an ad which merely appeared in someone's feed days before an unrelated purchase still gets credit. The wider the window, the more sales a platform can plausibly claim.

**View-through attribution.** A "view" can mean an ad scrolled past in under a second. Counting that as a contributing touch is how platforms inflate the top of the funnel. View-through conversions are the single easiest place for reported ROAS to detach from reality.

**The post-ATT modeling layer.** Since Apple's App Tracking Transparency changes, platforms lost much of their deterministic, person-level signal. To fill the gap, they model (read: estimate) conversions. Modeled conversions are useful directionally, but they are predictions dressed up as measured facts — and predictions reliably skew optimistic, because an optimistic number keeps you spending.

blocks.text: What "true ROAS" actually means
True ROAS is not a different formula. It's the same formula applied to de-duplicated revenue that reconciles to your bank.
The mental model is simple:
Trust the total first, then divide it up.

Most teams do the opposite. They trust each channel's self-reported number and then try to make the pieces fit. But four self-interested narrators will always sum to more than the truth. The disciplined approach is to anchor on the one number that can't lie — total revenue actually collected — and then allocate that finite pie across channels.

When you do this, two things happen. First, your blended ROAS drops, sometimes uncomfortably. Second — and this is the valuable part — your relative channel performance often reshuffles. The channel that looked like your hero on last-click frequently turns out to be coasting on demand other channels created.
How to find your real number (a practical sequence)
You don't need a data team to start. You need to stop trusting any single dashboard in isolation.

items: **Step 1 — Establish the ceiling.** Pull total revenue from your commerce platform (Shopify, etc.) for a fixed window. This is the most that all your channels combined could possibly have driven. It is the hard cap.

**Step 2 — Sum your platform claims.** Add up the revenue Meta, Google, TikTok, email, and everything else each reports for that same window. If the sum exceeds Step 1 — and it almost always will — the difference is your double-count gap, expressed in dollars.

**Step 3 — Calculate your inflation factor.** Divide total platform-claimed revenue by actual revenue. A factor of 1.31 means your blended reported ROAS is inflated by about 31%. Apply that haircut to each channel as a first-pass correction.

**Step 4 — Move from last-click to a reconciled view.** A simple, honest last-click model that ties every sale to a single channel will already beat the inflated sum-of-dashboards. From there, a unified attribution layer that de-duplicates across channels gets you to within a tight margin of truth.

Why this matters more than it sounds

An inflated ROAS isn't just a vanity problem. It actively misallocates your budget. If a channel looks like 4x but is really 2.5x because it's been borrowing credit, you'll keep pouring money into it while a quieter, genuinely efficient channel gets starved. You scale the wrong thing. You feel busy. Growth stalls and you can't see why.

Founders who fix attribution often don't increase spend at all — they just move existing budget toward channels that turned out to be doing the real work. The cheapest growth lever most D2C brands have is simply seeing clearly.

faq.a: Meta's ROAS is accurate as a measure of sales that touched a Meta ad inside its attribution window. It is not accurate as a measure of sales Meta caused, because it can't see the other channels that touched the same customer. Treat it as one input, not the verdict.

faq.q: Why is my reported revenue higher than my actual sales?
faq.a: Because each ad platform independently claims credit for sales involving multiple channels. The same purchase gets counted in several dashboards. Summing them produces revenue that was never collected.

faq.q: What's a realistic ROAS after correcting for double-counting?
faq.a: There's no universal number, but expect your blended figure to drop meaningfully once revenue is de-duplicated against your bank. A reported blended 4x commonly reconciles closer to 2.5–3x. The exact haircut depends on how much your channels overlap.

faq.q: How do I calculate true ROAS without a full data stack?
faq.a: Start by comparing total actual revenue to the sum of all platform-claimed revenue for the same window. The ratio is your inflation factor. Apply it as a haircut, then graduate to a unified attribution tool when you're ready for precision.
